rss.summary: Release: llm-gemini 0.37 Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family. It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme: Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00 From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00 Gemini 4 Hydrogen $1.50 $0.075 $7.50 Carbon and Argon are the same price , and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task. Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that. I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans . Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels: Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark. Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models: In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search. Tags: gemini , llm , google , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-pricing , ai , llms

rss.title: llm 0.37.2
rss.summary: Release: llm 0.37.2 Fixes a security issue reported by Daniel de Araujo in GHSA-v9h7-jj4g-f862 and GHSA-r639-rr7r-x72w . LLM has a mechanism called extra-openai-models.yaml - now managed by the new-in-0.37 llm openai endpoint add command - for using LLM with OpenAI-compatible API endpoints from other providers. Daniel reported two ways this could accidentally send your configured OpenAI API key to one of those providers: if the key named by api_key_name had never been stored, or if a responses: true model was run with -o chat_completions 1 . rss.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
rss.summary: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , gpus , claude-mythos-fable , recursive-self-improvement

I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo . The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud , for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. rss.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
rss.summary: Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send.
rss.text_excerpt:
Where does answer engine optimization (AEO) end and agent experience begin? Inside Resend, from the docs that help Claude Code pick an email API to the tools it uses to send. Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. rss.summary: NaiveAI could potentially top Artificial Analysis’s speed rankings. Our hands-on test suggests its coding quality holds up against DeepSeek.
rss.text_excerpt:
Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space. Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible . It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI , with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5 , which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog , this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40 . Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16 . The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4% . You pay for the checks either way. rss.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
rss.summary: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

# Atom — Open-source AI agents with built-in governance ### Train AI agents for the way your business works. **Teach agents your processes, give them relevant business context, and review the work—with built-in AI governance.** [![License: AGPL v3](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-AGPL_v3-blue.svg)](LICENSE.md) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.11%E2%80%933.13-blue)](docs/getting_started/quick-start.md) [![Local workflows](https://img.shields.io/badge/local_workflows-verified-green)](docs/acceptance/VERIFIER_ACCEPTANCE_2026-11-01.md) [Try locally](#try-atom-locally) · [See the workflows](docs/demo/VERIFIED_WORKFLOWS.md) · [What's verified](#what-you-can-rely-on) · [Report an issue](https://github.com/rush86999/atom/issues)
![Atom workspace](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/398de2e3-4ea6-487c-93ae-9600a66598fc) ## Start with a job you already do Atom helps you build AI agents around the way your team works: the files they use, the rules they follow, the output you expect and the decisions that need your approval. It is open source and self-hosted, with business automation and AI governance in the same platform. For example, give Atom a price list to prepare a quote, or check an invoice against purchase and receiving records, then produce a document showing the result. Inspect the source records, calculations and output before using it. **Open source and self-hosted.** Run your own copy and configure a supported local or hosted model. The starter sample below needs no model or cloud key. **Teach your rules. Review the work. Keep the context.** - **Turn company data into deliverables.** Demonstrated workflows map unfamiliar spreadsheet columns, calculate against source records and produce cited Word or PowerPoint documents within supported schemas. - **Make your rules reusable.** Save field mappings, commercial terms and contextual lessons. New work adopts accepted corrections; active work keeps its accepted teaching snapshot. - **Handle work that needs an answer.** Supported durable questions, approvals and waits survive restarts. Completed operations are retained, and uncertain effects need reconciliation before another attempt. - **Keep decisions reviewable.** Author ordered policies in the canvas editor. Supported deterministic rules retain unresolved requirements rather than inventing an approval. - [TRUNCATED]

支持日常实习、暑期实习、校招和社招 1–3 年；支持 Java、C++、Go 单语言或混合语言。 - 可选择六种面试官风格、严格或即时引导纠错模式，以及是否加入编码题。 - 可提供简历和岗位 JD，让项目深挖、技术题和最终反馈贴近目标岗位。 - 面试中记录已考察主题、薄弱点和待追问内容；支持暂停、恢复和提前结束。 - 技术知识库、面试官风格和评分规则放在该 skill 的 [references/](skills/backend-interview-simulator/references/) 中，按需加载。 安装后可以说： ```text 开始一场模拟面试。我是应届生，想练习 Java 后端面试。 ``` 面试中可以说“继续”“跳过”“结束”“换个风格”或“反馈”。 ## 简历批量出题：resume-interview-question-generator [查看 skill](skills/resume-interview-question-generator/SKILL.md) 候选人给出想分析的简历条目，AI 一次性生成主问题和追问文档，减少逐轮模拟面试的对话时间。只给项目/实习经历或只给专业技能都可以，不要求整份简历，也不限技术栈。 - 出题时只看面试官可见的简历条目。项目/实习题不受 JD 影响；专业技能题以简历为主，可少量加入 JD 强调但简历未写的技术问题，并标明来源。 - 先保存纯问题稿，再根据候选人的选择读取项目代码、文档等材料补充回答；材料中的隐藏细节不会反向变成面试题。 - 可选择“只要问题”或“问题和简短参考回答”；缺少依据的项目细节标为“待补充”。 - 按简历条目分组，主问题下列出可能的追问；默认在调用时当前工作目录的 `./resume/` 新建 UTF-8 Markdown 文档，不覆盖旧文件。 安装后可以说： ```text 根据下面这些简历条目，一次性生成面试主问题和追问文档：…… ``` 需要回答时可以直接说“问题和参考回答一起生成”，并提供项目代码、文档或补充说明。 ## 安装 把下面的请求发给支持 skills 的 AI 工具，让它安装并检查两个 skill： ```text 请安装 https://github.com/Hazenix/backend-interview-simulator 中的两个 skill： 1. skills/backend-interview-simulator/ 2. skills/resume-interview-question-generator/ 请将每个目录完整安装到当前工具的 skills 目录，并确认两个 skill 都能使用。 ``` 只需要其中一个时，在请求中明确指定对应的 skill 名称和目录。 ## 项目结构 ```text backend-interview-simulator/ ├── skills/ │ ├── backend-interview-simulator/ │ │ ├── SKILL.md # 逐轮模拟面试 │ │ └── references/ # 模拟面试所需的知识库与规则 │ └── resume-interview-question-generator/ │ └── SKILL.md # 简历批量出题 ├── README.md └── LICENSE ``` ## 贡献指南 欢迎补充题库、改进追问逻辑或修正文档。提交 PR 前请检查所改 skill 的触发范围和生成结果。题库内容可参照 [现有知识库](skills/backend-interview-simulator/references/common-backend-knowledge-base.md)。不要提交真实简历、项目代码或其他候选人资料。 ## 许可证与致谢 本项目采用 [MIT License](LICENSE)。技术知识库部分引用了 [JavaGuide](https://github.com/Snailclimb/JavaGuide) 的高频面试题整理，仅作为面试考察点使用，不改变其原有许可。感谢 JavaGuide 和 [xiaolincoding](https://xiaolincoding.com/) 提供的公开资料。

An AI coding teammate that moves into your Godot project.

> **It explores your repo, edits files, runs your tests, and shows you the diff — without leaving the app.** > > Every turn is a checkpoint, memory survives sessions, and MCP tools plug straight into the loop. ## 🖼️ Look inside ![GAI desktop coding agent](agent/asset/image/screenshot/gai_1.png)

Streaming tool calls, inline diffs, and token usage — the whole loop in one window.

Your own repository is never touched. - 💾 **Memory that persists.** During compaction a background agent curates `.memory/` — your rules, goals, and history — so the next session already knows. - 🖥️ **An editor, not a bystander.** File tree, tabs, images, Markdown preview, and a Git Bash window, one click from the chat. - 🔌 **MCP-ready.** Any MCP tool joins the built-in toolbox and shows up in the same streaming transcript. - 🛡️ **Local-first vision.** Attach an image to the request, or let MiniCPM-V describe it on your machine. The hub is the service that connects these interfaces to your sessions. **[Get started](docs/getting-started.md)** to install Evener, connect a model provider, and repair a small program with a check you can run yourself. These guides track **main**. The first-run guide uses the latest successful snapshot from main; tagged releases can lag the behavior described here. Start the service with `evener hub`. Its listener (`--addr`, `EVENER_HUB_LISTEN_ADDR`, or TOML `addr`), a client's destination (`--hub-url` or `EVENER_HUB_URL` where supported), and the advertised `public_url` are separate settings. Agent Asteroid

**Agent Asteroid is an open-source scanner for known, remotely exploitable vulnerabilities.** It checks internet-facing IP addresses, domains and links for the products and versions associated with those vulnerabilities, using read-only, non-destructive probes that do not change configuration or target state. It is also one of the scanners in the [Ostorlab KEV agent group](https://github.com/Ostorlab/KEV), which adds Nuclei, Tsunami, Nmap and Metasploit coverage. A credential-bypass check that confirms a public in-product secret is accepted submits only locally minted bearer tokens for a fabricated identity — asserting at most a read-only `user:read` claim — to non-sensitive identity or RBAC endpoints.
